name: Revolt of solitary instinct against social bonds
plain_explanation: Russell's central diagnosis: human beings are gregarious by self-interest but solitary by instinct, and romanticism is what happens when people throw off the 'prudent restraints of social behaviour' that keep the solitary instinct in check, producing an exhilarating but ultimately anti-social 'ecstasy of independence'.
precise_definition: The tendency, intensified by the romantic movement, to elevate the unfettered individual Ego and its passions above the compromises required for social cooperation, expressed philosophically as solipsism, ethically as self-development as the supreme principle, and politically as anarchism or despotism.
why_it_mattered: Russell uses it to explain both the psychological appeal of romanticism (a 'godlike exaltation' available otherwise only to mystics) and its dangerous political trajectory toward dictatorship, since 'if we could all live solitary... we could all enjoy this ecstasy of independence; since we cannot, its delights are only available to madmen and dictators.'
historical_origin: Traced by Russell to a permanent tension in human nature, newly given free rein by the romantic revolt against Christian and social restraint.
examples: Frankenstein's monster turning from a longing for love to systematic murder after rejection
D. H. Lawrence's 'The Man Who Loved Islands', whose hero dies of hunger and cold in pursuit of total isolation
The romantic conception of passionate love as a battle between egos (Strindberg, D. H. Lawrence)
objections: Man is not in fact a solitary animal, so self-realization cannot serve as the supreme principle of ethics so long as social life survives (Russell's own concluding objection)
competing_positions: Christianity's earlier (partial) taming of the Ego through religion and morality
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell connects it to German idealist solipsism, to nationalism (the nation as a corporate soul/ego), and ultimately to the anti-Semitic and anti-capitalist rhetoric found in Byron and later movements.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly tied by Russell to the rise of nationalism and to the anarchy-or-despotism dilemma he sees as romanticism's political legacy.
